title: Find a wall stud with a magnetic stud finder: slide it flat until it locks onto a hidden screw and let it hang
instruction: Find a stud behind the wall with the magnetic stud finder in its holder. Keep its back flat on the wall and slide it slowly over the wall until its magnets pull it onto a hidden screw, then let go so it hangs there.
context: Before hanging a shelf, a TV bracket or a heavy mirror on drywall, people look for a stud so that the screws bite into wood. A magnetic stud finder is the simplest tool for it: rare-earth magnets in a pocket-sized body, no batteries. Slid flat over the wall, it is tugged onto the steel screws that hold the drywall to each stud, which cannot be seen under the paint; the user feels the pull, lets go, and the finder hangs on the screw by itself, marking the stud. Lifted or tilted off the wall, its magnets are too far from a screw to catch it. Studs stand 16 in (406 mm) apart and the screws are at most 16 in apart up each stud, so a few slow passes along a wall find one.
setup:
Millimetres. x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the robot's left (+) or right (-) of the midline, z up from the table top; arm bases at y = +305 and -305. The finder is the only loose part.
Wall section, fixed (made for the trial: a full-thickness, true-size slice of an ordinary stud wall, only its height cut): one piece of 1/2 in (12.7) gypsum drywall, 660 long (y = -330 to +330) and 230 tall (z = 0 to 230), its face the plane x = 255, facing the robot, primed and painted flat white. Behind it: a pine 2x4 bottom plate laid flat (38 x 89), a 1/2 in plywood cap across the top (painted white, so the studs cannot be seen from above) and two kiln-dried pine 2x4 studs (38 x 89) between them, 16 in (406) apart on centre. The board is glued to the frame with construction adhesive and fixed with one drywall screw in each stud (#6 x 1-1/4 in coarse thread, steel, bugle head 8.3 across) on the stud's centre line; each head is driven 1.0 below the face, spotted with joint compound and painted over, so nothing on the face shows where the studs or screws are. No other steel within 50 of the face below the cap.
Four such sections are built, alike but for where the studs and screws are, and one is drawn at random for each trial (in simulation: the trial's seed mod 4). Left stud's centre y and both screws' height z: section 0: +190, 114; 1: +110, 126; 2: +150, 114; 3: +230, 126. The right stud is 406 to the right of the left one (y = -216, -296, -256, -176). Each section has its screw positions written on its back.
Stud finder, free: CH Hanson 03040 magnetic stud finder: black soft-rubber body 82 long, 32 across its two rounded ends and 20 deep, with a flat back; yellow side tabs (38 across them), two round yellow badges on its front with a rotating two-way level between them, and a yellow pointer loop at its lower end (90 long in all); 68 g (0.15 lb, maker). Two rare-earth magnets sit behind its back, one behind each badge, 25 above and below its centre.
Holder, fixed (made for the trial): grey ABS block 70 x 80 x 34 tall at x = 140 to 210, y = +260 to +340, with a slot 25 x 44 x 28 deep. The finder stands in it on its pointer, upright, back face toward +x (the wall) at x = 190, centred on y = +300, its top 96 above the table.
Start: finder in its holder; both grippers open at the ready pose.
Magnet (a stated force from the geometry, to be matched to the real finder): each magnet is taken as an N42 neodymium disc 12.7 across and 3.2 thick, 1.0 behind the back. Its field is computed from the disc's size; the screw head is a soft-steel pole whose flux is capped by saturation of the screw's 2.4 root. Flat on the wall (2.0 from magnet to head) this gives a pull onto the wall of 1.5 N straight over a screw, 1.1 N at 4 off its axis and none past 9, and a sideways pull toward the screw's axis of up to 0.8 N (at 6 off). No magnetic force elsewhere.
Friction (estimates): finder back on painted drywall 0.40 static, 0.35 sliding.
scoring:
Read at the end of the run (real trial: the final frame and a rule; the screws' positions are on the back of the section).
Flat on the wall: the finder's back within 2 of the wall's face plane at four points (each side of both badges), its lower badge below the wall's top.
On a screw: flat on the wall, and the centre of either badge (a magnet's centre) within 10 of a screw's axis, measured in the wall's plane.
Hanging: on a screw, its lowest point at least 20 above the table, no gripper within 30 of it for at least 1 s, and still (moved under 1 and 2 degrees over the last 1 s).
1.0: the finder hangs on either screw.
0.5: the finder is on a screw at least 20 above the table but not hanging (a gripper within 30 of it, or not yet still).
0.25: a gripper holds the finder flat on the wall at least 20 above the table, but not on a screw.
0: anything else, including the finder on the table, back in its holder, lying on the wall's top, leaning against the wall, held off the wall or tilted on it, or let go anywhere but over a screw (it falls).
Either stud counts. The finder may be dropped and picked up again; only the end state is scored.
run_limit: 3,600 steps (180 seconds at 20 Hz); the scripted demo needs 19 to 29 seconds, depending on where the screws are
reset_notes: Pull the finder straight off the wall (do not drag it across the paint) and stand it back in its holder, back toward the wall. Draw the next wall section at random and set it in the same place. Touch up the paint if the finder scuffs it.
fidelity: Rigid bodies. The finder is one rigid body of its measured outline. The studs behind the board are hidden and never touched, so only their screws are modelled, as points that the magnets pull toward. Each magnet's pull on a screw head is a stated force computed from the magnet's and screw's geometry (README), applied at the magnet; to be matched to the real finder by pulling it off a screw with a spring scale. Paint scuffing and pull on other steel are not modelled.
